tool.name: MDOWHillshade
tool.summary: Computes a Multi-Directional Oblique-Weighted (MDOW) hillshade from a single-band DEM, blending four sun directions so that every slope is lit obliquely (after Mark 1992). Correct on geographic (latitude/longitude) rasters, with optional hypsometric shading and vertical exaggeration.
tool.usage:
A traditional single-source hillshade emphasizes terrain that happens to be lit obliquely, but washes out structures that run parallel to the light: slopes facing directly toward the sun are uniformly bright and slopes facing directly away are uniformly dark, hiding the detail on both. The Multi-Directional Oblique-Weighted (MDOW) hillshade of Mark (1992) addresses this by computing four hillshades with sun directions fanned around your primary illumination direction (at -67.5, -22.5, +22.5 and +67.5 degrees from it) and blending them cell by cell, weighting each direction by the square of the sine of the angle between that direction and the cell's aspect. Each slope is therefore lit most strongly by the sun directions most oblique to it, revealing subtle relief in every orientation - an effect similar to the classic Swiss multiple-light-source style of relief shading. This tool computes the weights from each cell's own aspect (Mark's original image used an aspect surface generalized to 1-km cells; weighting by the exact aspect gives a crisper result at full resolution).
With the default primary direction of 270 (west), the four blended sun directions are 202.5, 247.5, 292.5 and 337.5 degrees. All four suns share the same inclination above the horizon (default 30 degrees, following Mark 1992). Output values run from 0 (fully shaded) up to one less than the number of gray levels (fully lit).
Unlike the standard hillshade, this tool is accurate for DEMs in geographic coordinate systems: the horizontal and vertical dimensions of each cell are recomputed for every row of the raster from the spheroid, so slopes and shading are correct at any latitude without projecting the DEM first. Projected DEMs use faster constant-cell planar formulas. Elevation units are read from the DEM's vertical coordinate system when one is defined (geographic DEMs are assumed to be in meters); otherwise the tool asks you to choose meters or feet.
Hypsometric shading darkens the hillshade at lower elevations: at a strength of s percent, the brightness multiplier grades from (100 - s) percent at the minimum elevation up to 100 percent at the maximum, adding an impression of overall relief.
This tool is one part of the classic "Swiss style" of relief presentation (after Eduard Imhof and the Swiss cartographers, whose hand-drawn conventions Kurt Brassel first automated), which combines three strategies: illuminating the terrain from multiple directions, elevation-based tone adjustments that mimic atmospheric perspective, and softening of the final image. In this toolbox the MDOW Hillshade and Multi-Sun Hillshade tools provide the multi-directional illumination, the hypsometric-shading options and the Simple Hypsometric Shading tool provide the elevation-based tinting, and the Blurred Hillshade tool provides the softening.
Environments. By default the output matches the input grid exactly (same extent, cell size, and coordinate system). Honored environments: Processing Extent, Snap Raster, Cell Size, and Output Coordinate System, all applied as finishing steps to the computed hillshade - the extent clips it (with the snap raster aligning the clip window), the cell size resamples it, and the output coordinate system reprojects it. Because the shading is always computed first from the full-resolution source DEM, cells at a clipped edge carry true hillshade values, and resampling or reprojecting smooths the finished shading rather than recomputing it on the new grid. The Mask environment is not honored, and pyramids are always built with bilinear resampling regardless of the Pyramid environment. The output carries statistics and a histogram so it renders correctly without a separate Calculate Statistics step. Symbolize the result with ArcGIS Pro's standard stretch renderers.
For a video walk-through of the MDOW method, see Jeff Jenness's lecture at https://youtu.be/DP309q778Vw
References: • Mark, R. K. (1992). A multidirectional, oblique-weighted, shaded-relief image of the Island of Hawaii. U.S. Geological Survey Open-File Report 92-422. https://pubs.usgs.gov/of/1992/of92-422/ • Horn, B. K. P. 1981. Hill shading and the reflectance map. Proceedings of the IEEE 69:14-47.

dialogReference.para: The elevation raster (DEM) to compute the hillshade from. It must be single band. Choose a raster from the map or browse to one on disk.
The output MDOW hillshade raster (integer, 0 to one less than the number of gray levels; NoData where the DEM has NoData or at the outer edge). A suggested name is filled in from the input.

The DEM's elevation units, Meters or Feet. Filled in and locked automatically when the DEM defines a vertical coordinate system; geographic DEMs are assumed to be in meters. You are only asked to choose when the DEM does not say.

The compass direction the four blended sun directions are centered on, 0 to 360 degrees clockwise from north. The four suns sit at -67.5, -22.5, +22.5 and +67.5 degrees from this direction; with the default of 270 (west, following Mark 1992) they are 202.5, 247.5, 292.5 and 337.5 degrees.

param.name: altitude
param.displayname: Inclination to sun, all directions (0-90 degrees)

dialogReference.para: The angle of the light sources above the horizon, 0 (grazing) to 90 (directly overhead) degrees, applied to all four sun directions. The default 30 follows Mark (1992).

The number of gray levels in the output: values run from 0 (fully shaded) to one less than this number (fully lit), each value covering an equal share of the illumination range. The default, 256, matches the standard Esri hillshade's 0 to 255. A small number gives a posterized cartographic look; with 32 or fewer levels the output also gets a raster attribute table listing each gray level and its cell count. A larger number gives a higher-precision hillshade, although the added precision may not be visually apparent on a computer screen.
Darkens the hillshade at lower elevations to add an impression of overall relief. The amount is set by the Hypsometric strength.

How strongly low elevations are darkened, 0 to 100 percent. At strength s, the brightness multiplier grades from (100 - s) percent at the minimum elevation up to 100 percent at the maximum. The default is 50.
Multiplies the elevations before shading, exaggerating (greater than 1) or flattening (less than 1) the relief. The default is 1 (no exaggeration).

scriptExample.title: MDOW Hillshade example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: MDOW hillshade of a geographic DEM with mild hypsometric shading.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.MDOWHillshade( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_WGS84", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_MDOW", elev_units="Meters", azimuth=270, altitude=30, levels=256, use_hypso=True, hypso_strength=40, vert_exag=1)

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Multi-Directional Oblique-Weighted hillshade (Mark 1992) with correct geodesic handling of geographic DEMs, hypsometric shading, and vertical exaggeration.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Computes a Multi-Directional Oblique-Weighted (MDOW) hillshade from a single-band DEM: four hillshades with sun directions fanned -67.5, -22.5, +22.5 and +67.5 degrees around the primary illumination direction are blended per cell with sine-squared aspect weights, so every slope is lit most strongly from the directions oblique to it - revealing terrain that a single-direction hillshade washes out. Cell dimensions on geographic DEMs are recomputed for every row from the spheroid, so shading is accurate at any latitude without projecting first; projected DEMs use planar formulas. Options: primary illumination direction, inclination of all four suns, number of gray levels, hypsometric shading that darkens low elevations, and vertical exaggeration. The output matches the input grid (honoring the Processing Extent, Snap Raster, Cell Size, and Output Coordinate System environments as post-computation finishing steps) and carries statistics and a histogram. Reference: Mark, R. K. (1992), USGS Open-File Report 92-422. Video introduction to the method: https://youtu.be/DP309q778Vw
